warnings.warning: Equation (1) visibly prints 1256, but that coefficient is incompatible with Figure 2's centimeter-scale tide curve unless an omitted decimal point or unit transformation is documented; the source value must be retained rather than silently repaired.
The tide fit does not publish the underlying observations, fitting method, residuals, time unit, coefficient units, or datum conversion needed to reproduce the 40- and 50-minute readings.
Equations (3)-(4) treat time derivatives of free-surface elevation as wave-particle speed and acceleration without the depth-dependent Airy velocity field or a justification for that proxy.
The Airy-wave branch assigns amplitude, wavelength, and period but omits water depth, dispersion verification, vertical coordinate, near-shore transformation, attenuation, and phase calibration.
Equation (5) borrows Morison inertia and drag terms without checking Reynolds and Keulegan-Carpenter regimes, partial submergence, porous finite geometry, or shape-specific coefficient applicability.
Equations (7)-(8) use the same undivided total wave force to define normal and shear stresses, without resolving load direction or the components acting on a stated failure plane.
The reduction to zero cohesion in Equation (9) omits effective stress, pore pressure, saturation, and moisture-dependent cohesion even though the later failure calculation is driven by wetting.

Equation (11), g(w)=-140w^2+56w+28.5, does not reproduce Figure 4 under an explicit shared water-content scale; the plotted maximum and later percentage readings therefore lack a coherent calibration record.
With f_0=0 and f_c=1, Equation (12) increases toward f_c, contrary to the text's description of f_c as a minimum reached after saturation; parameter order, units, and calibration are unresolved.
The paper equates Van Genuchten pressure head psi with Horton infiltration rate f(t), although pressure head and rate have different physical dimensions and roles.
Equation (14) does not fully state unit conversions, drop mass and density, branch continuity at 3 mm, or how one representative diameter stands for an event-level drop-size distribution.
Equation (15) gives d_50=2.52i^0.32, but Equation (16) substitutes i^0.23; the exponent conflict and transformed constants must be derived or corrected from source data before use.
The thresholds and constants in Equation (16) are not derived from Equations (14)-(15), and rainfall-intensity units, regression sample, fit error, and uncertainty are not supplied.

Equation (17), dP/dt=K_2Pr, has a positive sign while P is discussed as sand washed away or changing sand volume; P's state meaning, initial condition, integration, area conversion, and coefficient units are unresolved.
Equation (18), phi=0.8462w+5.256, introduces a second moisture-friction fit without explaining its relation to Equation (11), its water-content scale, fit observations, residuals, or valid domain.

global_organization_chain: Summary: unequal erosion question -> tide/wave/strength/moisture chain -> cuboid and aspect direction -> 15-percent mixture -> rain split -> ANSYS agreement
Front matter: beach foundation context -> four-task roadmap -> assumptions -> notation -> six equal-volume candidates
Dry physical chain: Sandy Hook tide -> Airy kinematics -> Morison force -> Mohr-Coulomb required angle
Moisture chain: quadratic capacity -> Horton rate -> Van Genuchten retention -> three-stage cuboid -> 50-minute crossing
Geometry decision: six-shape Table 1 -> cuboid -> length-width traversal -> narrow water-facing direction
Mixture decision: viable moisture range -> collapse-time traversal -> 5-percent maximum -> 15-percent compactness recommendation
Rain chain: intensity -> drop diameter/speed/energy/momentum -> scour and seepage -> rain friction fit -> Table 2 cuboid result
Verification and handoff: ANSYS field plots -> practical strategies -> strengths and limitations -> Article -> eighteen-source provenance ledger

main_argument_chains.claim: A tide boundary and wave model can produce the applied friction angle used in a sandcastle stability test.
main_argument_chains.decision_consequence: Use the required angle only after tide-scale, kinematic, coefficient, force-decomposition, and effective-stress repairs.

main_argument_chains.claim: Moisture evolution can be compared with the applied stress ratio to obtain a cuboid duration.
main_argument_chains.decision_consequence: Treat 50 minutes as an internal source result until hydraulic dimensions and the complete time trace are reproducible.

main_argument_chains.claim: A common tide-wave chain can compare six geometries and then refine the winning cuboid family.
main_argument_chains.decision_consequence: Retain cuboid as best of the six reported candidates and narrow-front as a direction, not a universal optimum.

main_argument_chains.claim: Initial moisture can be traversed to balance predicted duration against compactness.
main_argument_chains.decision_consequence: Carry both 67 and 64.43 minutes and require a formal or experimental tradeoff before calling 15 percent optimal.

main_argument_chains.claim: Rain can be decomposed into impact, scour, and infiltration before a second six-shape comparison.
main_argument_chains.decision_consequence: Use rainy effective heights only after exponent, sign, hydraulic handoff, scenario, and uncertainty repairs.

main_argument_chains.claim: ANSYS fields can provide a second computational view of the rain-conditioned shape result.
main_argument_chains.decision_consequence: Treat 'very similar' as presentation evidence until the project and a common quantitative metric are available.

main_argument_chains.claim: Mechanism findings can be translated into practical construction and environmental guidance.
main_argument_chains.decision_consequence: Keep the Article's advice conditional on the model boundaries and on field, safety, and environmental evidence.
